title: Steering vectors and activation engineering
summary: How adding or erasing a direction in a transformer's residual stream changes behavior: difference of means, layer and scale, ablation and LEACE, evaluation, a real lab, failure modes and newer methods.
outcomes: Compute a difference-of-means steering vector from contrast pairs and explain why averaging beats a single pair
Use cosine similarity and projection to measure how much of a concept an activation carries
Choose an injection layer, token positions and coefficient, judging scale against the residual stream norm
Apply directional ablation, weight orthogonalization and LEACE, and state what each guarantees
Design an evaluation that measures both the target behavior and capability side effects on held-out data
Build, sweep and evaluate a CAA vector on a small open chat model with forward hooks
Explain why mean effects can hide anti-steerable inputs and why prompting is the baseline to beat
Describe conditional, learned and persona-vector methods and the problem each one addresses

lessons.title: Steering by adding a vector to the residual stream

blocks.md:
Suppose you want a chat model to be less sycophantic (agreeing with or flattering the user instead of being accurate), to talk more positively, or to refuse less often. The usual tools are **prompting** (cheap, but it uses context and the model may ignore it) and **fine-tuning** (reliable, but it needs labeled data, compute and a new set of weights for every behavior).

**Activation engineering** is a third option: leave the weights and the prompt alone, and edit the model's internal activations during the forward pass. Turner et al. coined the term and showed that a single added vector can shift the topic or sentiment of GPT-2-XL's output (the largest GPT-2, with 1.5 billion parameters).

Recall the GPT you built. Each token position carries a vector of size $d_{\text{model}}$, the **residual stream**. Every block reads it and adds its result back:

$x_{l+1} = x_l + \text{attn}_l(x_l) + \text{mlp}_l(x_l)$ (simplified; the real block applies the MLP after the attention update).

Because the stream is a running sum, anything you add at layer $l$ is visible to every later layer and to the **unembedding**, the final matrix that turns the last residual vector into one score (logit) per vocabulary token, like the output head of your GPT. That makes it a natural place to intervene.

blocks.caption: Activation addition: at layer l, add a fixed steering vector v scaled by a coefficient c to the residual stream. Positive c strengthens the property v encodes, negative c suppresses it.

blocks.md:
Why would one fixed vector do anything sensible? The **linear representation hypothesis** says high-level concepts (sentiment, language, the gender of a word, whether a request is harmful) are encoded as directions in activation space. A **linear probe** is a simple linear classifier (a weight vector and a threshold) trained on activations to predict whether a concept is present: it reads a concept out, while steering puts one in.

Park et al. make this precise in two spaces. The *output space* holds the unembedding vectors, one per vocabulary token; a concept there is a direction such as queen minus king, parallel to woman minus man, and it is what a probe measures. The *input space* holds the context vectors the model computes, the ones steering edits. Their result in one line: adding a concept's input-space direction raises the log-odds of that concept's tokens and leaves the odds of independent concepts unchanged.

Here is that statement in miniature. Take a model with 3-dimensional vectors and four output tokens whose unembedding vectors are king (-1, -1, 1), queen (1, -1, 1), roi (-1, 1, 1) and reine (1, 1, 1): coordinate 0 encodes gender, coordinate 1 encodes language. Each token's logit is the dot product of its unembedding vector with the final context vector x, and softmax turns logits into probabilities. Start from x = (-0.5, -1, 2) and add the gender direction (1, 0, 0), once and then twice.

blocks.title: Adding a gender direction to a toy context vector

scenes.caption: Unsteered: logits 3.5, 2.5, 1.5, 0.5. The model favours the English masculine word king (0.644).
Add (1, 0, 0). The log-odds of queen over king go from -1 to +1, but French over English stays -2 for both genders (roi vs king, reine vs queen).
Add it twice: queen over king is now +3 and queen reaches 0.839, while the language odds are still exactly -2. Simplified: a real edit happens mid-network and passes through more layers.

blocks.md:
**ActAdd** (Activation Addition, Turner et al.) is the simplest recipe. Pick a contrast pair of prompts, for example "Love" and "Hate". Run each through the model and record the residual stream $h_+^l$ and $h_-^l$ just before layer $l$. The steering vector is $c\,(h_+^l - h_-^l)$. While the model processes a user prompt, add it to the residual stream at the same layer and let the forward pass continue.

No gradient step is involved and one pair of prompts is enough, so iterating is fast: the authors report finding most of their contrast pairs in minutes.

Note that $h_+^l$ is not one vector but one per token, so the ActAdd vector is a short *sequence*. The two prompts often tokenize to different lengths; ActAdd right-pads the shorter one with whitespace tokens until they match, then subtracts position by position. The resulting sequence is added to the first positions of the user prompt (front alignment), so only those few positions are edited directly and every later token sees the change through attention. The authors report that aligning the addition later in the prompt steers more strongly, but editing the very last position reliably broke syntax.

blocks.title: ActAdd: one contrast pair, one added vector

scenes.caption: Run the two contrast prompts through the frozen model and cache the residual stream just before layer l. Nothing is trained.
Subtract the two cached activations and scale by c. What the prompts share cancels; what differs (roughly, love versus hate) remains.
Now run the user's prompt. Its residual stream flows through the lower layers untouched.
At layer l the vector is added to the stream, and every later layer reads the shifted activation. The output drifts toward the positive side of the pair.

blocks.md: A steering vector edits **activations**, not weights and not the prompt. It is computed once, before inference, and the same vector is added on every forward pass while it is switched on.

blocks.prompt: Turner et al. also injected a random vector, scaled to the same per-position norm as their working Anger minus Calm vector at c = +1. Predict: does the random vector change the completions as much as the steering vector does?
blocks.reveal:
No. The random vector did not noticeably change the qualitative distribution of completions. Even a random vector with the norm of the c = +10 steering vector shifted the outputs but left them about as coherent as the unsteered model.

So the effect comes from the **direction**, not merely from pushing the activations by a large amount. A good steering experiment always includes this random-direction control.

blocks.question: Why can a vector added only at layer l change the model's next-token prediction?
options: Because the model recomputes all earlier layers after the addition
Because the residual stream is a running sum: later layers read the shifted stream and the unembedding reads its final value
Because the vector is also added to the weights of every later layer
It cannot; the vector must be added at the last layer to matter
blocks.explain: Each block adds its output to the stream it reads, so a vector added at layer l stays in the sum. Later attention and MLP layers read it and react to it, and the final stream is what the unembedding decodes. No weights change and earlier layers are not rerun.

blocks.question: What does ActAdd need in order to build a steering vector?
options: A labeled dataset of a few thousand examples and a few gradient steps
A trained linear probe on the target concept
One pair of contrasting prompts and two forward passes
Access to the model's training data
blocks.explain: ActAdd is optimization-free: two forward passes on a prompt pair such as Love and Hate, a subtraction, and a scale factor. CAA (lesson 2), ITI (inference-time intervention, developed independently of ActAdd, slightly earlier) and the reading vectors of RepE (representation engineering) use more examples to get a cleaner direction; none of these fine-tunes the model.

lessons.title: Difference of means: building a vector from contrast pairs

blocks.md:
A single prompt pair is noisy. "Love" minus "Hate" captures sentiment, but also whatever else happens to differ between those two token sequences. **Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA)** by Panickssery (published as Rimsky) et al. fixes this by averaging over many pairs.

Each CAA pair is the same multiple-choice question with an answer letter appended. The positive prompt ends with the letter that shows the behavior (for example the sycophantic answer), the negative prompt ends with the other letter. The activation is read at the answer-letter position, so the two prompts in a pair differ by a single token.

blocks.caption: The mean-difference (MD) vector at layer l: the average of the pair differences, which equals the mean of the positive activations minus the mean of the negative ones.

blocks.md: In words: D is the set of pairs. Each pair is a question p with either the positive answer letter $c_p$ or the negative letter $c_n$ appended (letters, not the coefficient c), and $a_l$ is the residual activation at layer l at that letter. Every positive and every negative activation appears exactly once in the sum, so by linearity the average of the differences is the average of the positives minus the average of the negatives, $\mu_+ - \mu_-$.

Let us build one by hand. Take a toy residual stream with $d_{\text{model}} = 6$ and four pairs. Each pair shares a content vector; the positive member adds a hidden concept direction $(1, 0, 0.5, 0, 0, -0.5)$, the negative member subtracts it, and each activation also carries a little unrelated noise. (Simplified: real activations have thousands of dimensions and we would not know the true direction.) We will judge the result by its **cosine similarity** with the hidden direction: 1 when two vectors point the same way, 0 when they are perpendicular, minus 1 when they are opposite (the formula comes after the table).

blocks.title: Toy residual activations at the answer token

scenes.caption: Eight cached activations: four positive (P) and four negative (N). Row Pi and row Ni come from the same question with a different answer letter.
Dimension d0 already separates the classes: every P row is at least 0.5 there and every N row is 0 or below. But single dimensions can mislead; the concept is spread over d0, d2 and d5.
d5 points the other way: N rows sit higher. A good direction must combine dimensions with the right signs, which is exactly what subtracting the means does.

blocks.title: Difference of means, step by step

scenes.caption: Average the four positive rows column by column.
Average the four negative rows the same way.
Subtract. Content shared within each pair cancels, and much of the noise averages out. The result has length |v| = 2.368.
Divide by the length to get the unit direction used for measuring and ablating. Its cosine similarity with the hidden concept direction is 0.991.

blocks.md:
Two measurements appear everywhere in this field. The **cosine similarity** of two vectors a and b, written $\cos(a, b)$, is their dot product divided by the product of their two lengths, so it compares directions and ignores length. The **projection** $a \cdot \hat v$, where $\hat v$ is the unit vector you get by dividing v by its own length, says how far along the direction an activation sits, in the same units as the residual stream.

Projecting our eight activations onto $\hat v$ gives a one-number concept score for each. CAA uses the same idea to visualize which tokens in a real response align with a steering vector.

blocks.title: Projection of each activation onto the direction

scenes.caption: Onto the mean-difference direction: positives score 0.528 to 1.979, negatives score -1.531 to -0.475. A threshold at the midpoint of the class means (0.142) separates all eight.
Onto the direction from pair 4 alone (an ActAdd-style single pair): N1 now scores only -0.109, almost on the boundary. One pair's noise is baked into the direction.

blocks.title: Cosine with the hidden concept direction

scenes.caption: Each single-pair difference points roughly the right way, with cosines from 0.891 to 0.968 to the true direction.
The mean difference reaches 0.991, better than every individual pair. With hundreds of pairs, as in CAA, the gain is larger.

blocks.md:
Other methods extract the direction differently:

- **RepE** (representation engineering, Zou et al.) runs PCA (principal component analysis, which finds the direction of largest variance) on differences of activation pairs and calls the first principal component the *reading vector*; they report 5 to 128 stimuli is typically enough.
- **ITI** (inference-time intervention, Li et al.) works per attention head: it trains a linear probe on each head, keeps the top K heads by probe accuracy, and shifts each along a truthful direction by $\alpha$ times the activations' standard deviation along it.
- **Arditi et al.** take the difference of means between harmful and harmless instructions to find a refusal direction (lesson 4).

ITI targets truthfulness, measured on **TruthfulQA**: 817 questions written so that a popular misconception tempts a wrong answer. An answer counts as *true* if it asserts no falsehood and *informative* if it actually answers ("I have no comment" is true but not informative); ITI's headline score, true-times-informative, multiplies the true score by the informative score, so a model cannot score well by declining to answer. To avoid tuning on the questions they score, ITI uses 2-fold cross-validation: split the questions in half, find the directions on one half, score the other half, then swap.

The best direction to **classify** with is not always the best direction to **steer** with. ITI compared both on LLaMA-7B (Meta's open model with 7 billion parameters): shifting along the probe's weight vector scored 34.8% true-times-informative on TruthfulQA, while shifting along the mass mean shift (difference of means) scored 42.3%. A probe can lean on any feature that happens to separate the classes, causal or not.

blocks.title: ITI on LLaMA-7B: which direction to shift along

scenes.caption: TruthfulQA true-times-informative score, each direction with its own best strength (2-fold cross-validation). The difference-of-means direction wins clearly; a random direction barely moves the score.

blocks.question: You build a CAA vector from 300 pairs where every positive prompt happens to be longer than its negative partner. What is the most likely problem?
options: None: averaging over 300 pairs removes all confounds
The vector partly encodes prompt length, because that difference is consistent across pairs and does not average out
The vector will have length zero
Mean difference only works with exactly one pair
blocks.explain: Averaging cancels differences that vary randomly across pairs. A difference that is the same in every pair, such as length, survives averaging and becomes part of the vector. CAA avoids this by making each pair identical except for one answer letter.

blocks.question: In the toy example, the single-pair direction from pair 4 still classifies all eight activations correctly. Why prefer the mean difference anyway?
options: It is the only direction with unit length
It makes projections of negatives exactly zero
Single-pair vectors cannot be added to the residual stream
It is closer to the true concept direction (cosine 0.991 vs 0.891), so steering along it changes less of everything else
blocks.explain: Classification only needs the right sign. Steering adds the whole vector, including its off-concept components. Pair 4's direction has a larger share of noise, so adding it would also push unrelated dimensions. The averaged vector is cleaner.

lessons.title: Where to add it, at which tokens, and how hard

blocks.md: A steering vector has three knobs: the **layer** where it is added, the **token positions** it is added to, and the **coefficient** $c$. None of them has a universal default, so every paper in this course sweeps them on held-out data.

**Layer.** Too early and the concept may not exist yet as a direction; too late and few layers remain to act on it. CAA found that behavioral clustering of the A/B activations emerges about one third of the way through Llama 2 Chat's layers, and their layer sweep peaked at layer 13 and its neighbors in the 7B model and at 14 or 15 in the 13B model.

ActAdd likewise found middle layers most effective, with the best layer depending on how abstract the concept is: the Love vector worked best at layer 6 of GPT-2-XL, the more abstract Conspiracy vector at layer 23.

blocks.title: Sweeping the injection layer

scenes.caption: Simplified picture of a layer sweep: build a vector at each layer, add it at that layer, and score the behavior on held-out prompts.
Early injection: CAA's PCA plots show A/B activations separating by behavior only after a certain depth (for refusal in Llama 2 7B Chat, the clustering appears suddenly at layer 10).
Middle injection gives the largest effect in CAA's sweeps (layer 13 in the 7B model). ActAdd's wedding vector already works at the first layer of GPT-2-XL, peaks at layer 6, then declines.

Late injection is close to editing output tokens directly. Arditi et al. excluded layers beyond 0.8L (80 percent of the depth, where L is the number of layers) so a refusal direction could not simply be the unembedding of words like I.

blocks.md:
**Positions.** ActAdd adds its short sequence at the front of the user's prompt (lesson 1). CAA adds its vector at every token position after the user's prompt, so each generated token is steered. Arditi et al. add their refusal vector at one layer but at all positions.

**Coefficient.** What matters is the vector's size *relative* to the residual stream it joins. Watch what adding $c\,v$ does to the held-out toy activation $x = (0.5, 1, 0, 0.5, 0.5, -0.5)$, which has length (norm) 1.414 and projection $x \cdot \hat v = 0.686$.

blocks.tex: \cos(x + c\,v,\; v) = \frac{p + c\|v\|}{\sqrt{\|x\|^2 - p^2 + (p + c\|v\|)^2}}, \qquad p = x\cdot \hat v
blocks.caption: Adding c v grows only the component of x along v, from p to p plus c times the norm of v; the part of x perpendicular to v is untouched. As c grows the steered vector points almost entirely along v.

blocks.md: Where this comes from: split x into its projection p along $\hat v$ plus a part perpendicular to v, whose squared length is the squared length of x minus $p^2$. Adding $c\,v$ only grows the along-v part, and the cosine is that along-v part divided by the total length. With the toy numbers at c = 1: 0.686 + 2.368 = 3.054, the perpendicular part squared is 2 minus 0.471 = 1.529, so the cosine is 3.054 over the square root of 10.856, which is 0.927.

blocks.title: How fast the steering vector takes over the stream

curves.label: share of squared norm along v

scenes.caption: Toy numbers: at c = 1 the steered vector already has cosine 0.927 with v, and at c = 4 it is 0.993. Simplified: real models also normalize the stream and react nonlinearly.
Make the stream ten times longer (norm 14.1), as at a deeper layer where residual norms are larger. The same c now barely moves the direction: scale has to be judged against the local norm.
Back to the toy stream. Past a point the original content is a rounding error; this is where generations lose coherence.
show: share of squared norm along v

blocks.md: Real models show the same picture. In ActAdd, the Anger minus Calm vector was effective at $c = +10$, which made the intervention nearly ten times the norm of the ordinary forward pass; the authors' rough reading is that about 90% of the stream is then the steering vector. They also note that intervention strengths are typically below 15 in magnitude. CAA reports that larger multipliers degraded open-ended text, as judged by GPT-4 and by human readers, so they limited the range.

blocks.prompt: ActAdd measured that residual-stream norms are much smaller in early layers than in later ones. Predict: if you take a vector extracted at layer 2 and add it, unchanged, at layer 20, will its effect be stronger or weaker than adding it at layer 2?
blocks.reveal: Weaker, all else equal. The vector's norm stays the same but the stream it joins at layer 20 is much longer, so its share of the stream shrinks, exactly like the second plot scene. ActAdd tried this transplant: completions became noticeably angrier, but less so than with the vector extracted at layer 20 itself (the authors also credit the gap to work done by layers 0 and 1). The practical rule: add a vector at the layer it was extracted from, or rescale it to the local norm.

blocks.md: **Feature steering with sparse autoencoders.** Templeton et al. trained sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on the middle-layer residual stream of Claude 3 Sonnet, giving millions of interpretable feature directions. A **sparse autoencoder** is a small network trained to rewrite each activation as a weighted sum of a large dictionary of learned directions, with almost all weights zero. Its encoder computes nonnegative feature activations, its decoder adds up the matching decoder vectors to rebuild the activation, and training minimizes the reconstruction error plus a sparsity penalty on the feature activations. Because each activation uses only a few features, a feature often matches one human-readable concept. That is all this course needs; the separate Sparse autoencoders course (not a prerequisite) covers training and evaluation in depth.

To steer, they split the stream into SAE reconstruction plus error, clamp one feature to a chosen value, keep the error term (whatever the SAE fails to reconstruct, so nothing else is lost), and apply this at every token position.

Clamping the Golden Gate Bridge feature to 10 times its maximum observed activation made the model self-identify as the bridge; Anthropic ran this as the public Golden Gate Claude demo for 24 hours in May 2024. Interesting effects typically needed values outside the observed range, and extreme clamps (around 100 times) produced nonsense.

In code, both edits are **forward hooks**. In PyTorch, a function registered on a module with `register_forward_hook` is called with that module's output on every forward pass, and if it returns a value, that value replaces the output. So you can change activations without touching the model's code or weights, and remove the hook to get the original model back.

blocks.title: Steering and ablation hooks in PyTorch
blocks.code:
# helper (not shown): acts() runs the model, caches resid at layer L
pos = acts(model, pos_prompts, layer=L)   # [n, d_model]
neg = acts(model, neg_prompts, layer=L)   # [n, d_model]

v = pos.mean(0) - neg.mean(0)             # difference of means
v_hat = v / v.norm()

def add_hook(module, args, output):
    h = output[0] if isinstance(output, tuple) else output
    h += c * v                            # every position
    return output

def ablate_hook(module, args, output):
    h = output[0] if isinstance(output, tuple) else output
    h -= (h @ v_hat).unsqueeze(-1) * v_hat
    return output

layer = model.model.layers[L]
handle = layer.register_forward_hook(add_hook)
out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=60)
handle.remove()

scenes.caption: Cache residual activations at layer L for the positive and negative prompts (here the four toy pairs).
Difference of means and its unit vector, exactly the toy numbers from lesson 2.
The addition hook edits the layer's output in place. Simplified: it steers every position, while CAA adds only from the end of the prompt onward.
The ablation hook removes each position's component along v_hat (lesson 4). Its projection becomes 0 whatever it was.
Register the hook on decoder layer L, generate, then remove it so later calls run the unmodified model.

blocks.md: The trace uses toy numbers and hides three things a real model forces on you (lesson 6 runs them): a decoder layer's output was a tuple (hidden state first) in older transformers releases and is a plain tensor in current ones, hence the isinstance check; a chat template adds system and role tokens, which shifts every position; and a tokenizer may merge the answer letter with its bracket. Find positions by tokenizing.

blocks.question: A vector extracted at layer 6 of a 48-layer model works well at c = 4. A colleague adds the same vector at layer 40 with c = 4 and sees almost no effect. What is the most likely explanation?
options: At layer 40 the residual stream is much larger, so the same c is a much smaller relative push, and the concept may be represented differently there
Steering vectors only work in the first half of a network
Adding at a later layer reverses the sign of the vector
The model detects the vector and removes it
blocks.explain: Residual norms grow with depth, so a fixed-size vector becomes relatively small; on top of that, a direction found at layer 6 need not be the direction the concept uses at layer 40. Extract and inject at the same layer, and sweep c relative to the local norm.

blocks.question: Why do Golden Gate style feature clamps need values far above the feature's observed maximum?
options: Because the SAE decoder vectors have zero norm
The authors suspect the single clamped feature is normally co-active with several related features, so it must be pushed harder on its own
Because clamping only works at the last token
Because the error term cancels the clamp
blocks.explain: Templeton et al. suggest that in natural text a feature fires together with correlated features of related meaning. Steering one of them alone needs a stronger push to produce the same downstream effect. Push too far (around 100 times) and the model devolves into nonsense.

lessons.title: Directional ablation: what erasing the refusal direction reveals

blocks.md: Adding a vector pushes every activation by the same amount. Sometimes you want something else: remove a concept entirely, however much of it each activation contains. Arditi et al. did this for **refusal**. Across 13 open-source chat models up to 72B parameters they found a single direction such that erasing it stops the model refusing harmful requests, while adding it makes the model refuse even harmless ones.

They built the direction with the same difference of means as lesson 2. The training sets are 128 harmful instructions (from AdvBench, MaliciousInstruct and TDC2023, public collections of harmful requests used to test attacks on chat models) and 128 harmless ones (from Alpaca, a public set of about 52,000 everyday instructions released by Stanford); separate 32-instruction validation sets (harmful ones from HarmBench, a standardized red-teaming benchmark) are kept for choosing the direction. Activations are read at the **post-instruction** tokens, the chat-template tokens after the user's message, where the model is about to decide how to answer. Each position $i$ and layer $l$ gives a candidate $r_i^{(l)}$, so the number of candidates to choose from is the number of positions times the number of layers.

blocks.caption: Directional ablation: r-hat transpose x is the projection, how much of the direction x carries. Times r-hat it becomes that component as a vector; subtracting it leaves projection exactly 0. Applied at every layer and position.

blocks.md: Ablation changes harmless prompts too, so the authors measure how much it changes the model's predictions there with the **Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence**. It compares two probability distributions over the same outcomes: here P is the original model's next-token distribution and Q the edited model's. For each token, take the log of how much more likely P makes it than Q, weight that by P's probability, and add up over the vocabulary. The result is 0 exactly when the two distributions agree and grows as the edited model moves probability away from what the original predicted.

blocks.caption: KL divergence: the sum over tokens t of P of t times the log of P of t over Q of t.

blocks.title: Ablating and adding the direction in the toy stream

scenes.caption: Reuse the toy direction as r-hat and take the positive activation P2. Its projection is r-hat dot x = 1.583: plenty of the concept is present.
Subtract 1.583 times r-hat. Every coordinate changes a little, and the projection of x' onto r-hat is now exactly 0. Its norm drops from 2.179 to 1.498.
Ablation is not subtraction of a fixed amount. The negative activation N1 had projection -0.475; ablation moves it up to 0 too. Harmless activations change, which is why harmless KL is checked.

The opposite move: add v (length 2.368) to the negative N3. Its projection goes from -1.346 to 1.023, past the positive class's 0.528 minimum. This is how adding the refusal direction induces refusal.

blocks.prompt: Arditi et al. ablate the direction at every layer, not just the one it was extracted from. Predict why ablating at a single layer might not be enough.
blocks.reveal: Later attention and MLP layers can write the direction back into the stream. Erasing it at layer $l$ removes what is present at $l$, but a later block that reads other features (the harmful content itself is still in the stream) may recompute it. Ablating at every layer and position, or equivalently making every writer unable to write it, closes that gap. Addition, by contrast, only needs one layer: the added vector persists in the running sum.

blocks.md: **Weight orthogonalization.** The same ablation can be baked into the weights. Every matrix that writes to the residual stream (token embedding, positional embedding, attention output, MLP output, plus their output biases) gets its column vectors projected away from $\hat r$. Then no component can ever write along $\hat r$, and the edited model behaves like the ablated one with no runtime hooks. Arditi et al. show the two are equivalent and present this as a white-box jailbreak. A **jailbreak** gets a model to comply with requests it was trained to refuse; *white-box* means the attack needs direct access to the weights, which open-weights models give anyone.

blocks.caption: Weight orthogonalization: apply the same projection to every column of an output matrix, so whatever the matrix writes into the residual stream has zero component along r-hat.

blocks.title: Orthogonalizing a toy output matrix

scenes.caption: A toy 6 x 3 output projection W. Its columns have projections 0.844, 0 and 0.607 onto r-hat, so inputs to columns 0 and 2 write along the refusal direction.
After W' = W - r-hat r-hat-transpose W, every column has projection 0. Column 1 was already orthogonal and is unchanged. For z = (1, 0.5, -1), W'z equals the ablation of Wz exactly.

blocks.md: Why are the two edits equivalent? Follow the stream from the bottom. The orthogonalized embedding writes nothing along $\hat r$, so the stream starts with projection 0. Each block then adds $W_{\text{out}}' t$, whose projection on $\hat r$ is 0 by construction, so by induction the projection stays 0 at every layer and position, which is exactly what the ablation hooks enforce. Normalization layers (LayerNorm, RMSNorm) only read the stream to feed attention and the MLP and never add to it, so they need no edit.

How was one direction picked from all the candidates? Each is scored on separate validation sets: how much ablating it reduces refusal on harmful prompts (bypass score), whether adding it induces refusal on harmless prompts, and the KL divergence it causes on harmless prompts when ablated. The chosen direction minimizes the bypass score subject to: induce score above 0, KL below 0.1, and layer below 0.8L, where L is the number of layers. Refusal is then judged on JailbreakBench's 100 harmful instructions in two ways: a **refusal score** (does the reply contain a stock phrase such as "I'm sorry" or "As an AI") and a **safety score** (does Llama Guard 2, an open classifier model from Meta that labels a conversation safe or unsafe, rate the reply safe).

blocks.title: Choosing the refusal direction

nodes.label:
diff of means per
position and layer

scenes.caption: Every post-instruction position and every layer yields a candidate vector from the training split.
Filters on a separate validation split: it must induce refusal when added, must barely change harmless behavior when ablated, and must not sit next to the unembedding.
Among survivors, keep the one whose ablation most reduces refusal. The evaluation sets are kept disjoint from both splits.

blocks.md: Read this as an evaluation finding, not a technique to apply. One direction carries refusal in open-weights chat models, so anyone holding the weights can remove it with little effect on other capabilities; the authors read this as evidence that current safety fine-tuning is brittle. For evaluators, a model's refusal rate says little about the risk of releasing its weights. Adversarial suffixes (token strings found by automated search) work partly by suppressing this same direction.

What does ablation actually guarantee? Belrose et al. answer this for linear readers. Call a concept **linearly guarded** in a set of activations when no linear classifier predicts it better than a constant guess, under any convex loss such as the logistic loss. They prove this holds exactly when every class has the same mean activation.

So ablating the difference-of-means direction of the very activations you erase does guard the concept: it removes the only component in which the two means differ. Ablating any other direction (a probe's weights, a single pair's difference, a direction found at another layer) can leave a mean gap a probe will find.

blocks.caption: LEACE: center x, whiten it with W (the inverse square root of the activation covariance), project onto the directions correlated with the concept Z, unwhiten with the pseudo-inverse, subtract.

blocks.md: Among all affine edits that guard the concept, **LEACE** (least-squares concept erasure) moves the activations the least, measured by mean squared distance. For a binary concept the cross-covariance $\Sigma_{XZ}$ is a single column proportional to $\mu_+ - \mu_-$, so LEACE also moves every point along the mean difference; what changes is how far. Ablation sets every point's projection onto the mean difference to 0. LEACE instead zeroes the projection measured in whitened coordinates, which is the score of the least-squares linear predictor of the label, so each point moves a different distance and its plain projection need not become 0. Belrose et al. apply it layer after layer through a model (concept scrubbing).

blocks.title: Three erasures of the toy concept (8 activations)

scenes.caption: Distance between the class means. Ablating the single-pair direction from lesson 2 leaves a gap of 1.094; ablating the mean difference or applying LEACE leaves 0.
Training accuracy (%) of a logistic-regression probe fit on the edited points. With equal means its best fit is a constant, which scores 50% on these balanced classes.
Mean squared edit per activation. Both guarded edits remove the concept, but LEACE moves the points less (1.425 vs 1.653).

blocks.md: The guarantee is narrow. It covers linear classifiers, the activations whose means you computed, and the population those means stand for. A nonlinear probe may still recover the concept, a direction estimated on one split or layer is only approximately right on another, and refusal ablation applies one layer's direction at every layer, where it is not that layer's mean difference.

blocks.question: Arditi et al. compared two ways of removing the refusal direction. Option A subtracts the refusal vector (x minus r) at one layer. Option B ablates r-hat at every layer. Both bypassed refusal comparably. What is B's advantage on harmless prompts?
options: B is faster at inference
B also improves MMLU (a multiple-choice knowledge benchmark, lesson 5)
A shifts every activation by a fixed amount, pushing harmless ones far past zero; B only removes what is there, so it raised loss on harmless data less
There is no difference on harmless prompts
blocks.explain: Subtraction moves all activations by the same vector, so prompts with little refusal content end up strongly negative along r, an unnatural state. Ablation sets the component to zero regardless. In the paper's comparison, activation addition in the negative direction caused higher loss on harmless data than directional ablation.

blocks.question: Arditi et al. show that orthogonalizing the residual-stream writers against r-hat gives the same model as ablating r-hat at every layer. Why does this equivalence matter for interpretability?
options: It shows one direction, carried through the whole stream, accounts for refusal: no layer can rebuild it once no writer can write along r-hat
It shows refusal is stored in the unembedding matrix
It proves the direction is the only feature the model uses for safety in every context
It shows LayerNorm computes the refusal decision
blocks.explain: Every write to the stream goes through the embeddings, attention outputs and MLP outputs. If none can write along r-hat, the projection stays 0 at every layer (the induction argument above), and refusal still disappears. So the behavior runs through that one direction. It does not prove it is the only safety feature in every context (lesson 7 shows the limits). Norm layers only read the stream.

blocks.question: You ablate a direction found as the harmful minus harmless mean difference at layer 12, at every layer. A fresh linear probe trained at layer 20 still separates harmful from harmless prompts. What does this show?
options: Nothing contradictory: the guarantee only covers the activations whose class means defined the direction; at layer 20 the means can differ along other directions
The ablation code must be broken, because ablation makes every concept unreadable at every layer
Linear probes always succeed, whatever edit is applied
LEACE would have made the concept unreadable at every layer at once
blocks.explain: Equal class means, and so linear guardedness, holds for the activations the mean difference was computed on. Later layers recompute features from everything else in the stream, and their class means can differ along new directions. LEACE has the same scope; concept scrubbing fits a separate eraser at each layer in turn.

lessons.title: Side effects and how to evaluate a steering vector

blocks.md:
A steering result has two halves. Did the **target behavior** move, on prompts not used to build the vector? And what **else** moved: general knowledge, fluency, behavior on unrelated prompts? Good papers report both, and the tradeoff between them sets the usable coefficient.

The first example is from CAA, which built vectors for seven behaviors in Llama 2 Chat: AI coordination, corrigibility, hallucination, myopic reward, survival instinct, sycophancy and refusal. **Corrigibility** means a model's willingness to accept correction, or a change to its goals, from the people overseeing it.

blocks.title: CAA on top of system prompts (Llama 2 13B Chat, corrigibility)

scenes.caption: Average probability of the corrigible answer on held-out A/B questions, steering at layer 13 with no system prompt. Steering moves it from 0.57 down to 0.45 or up to 0.83.
With a system prompt asking for the behavior, the baseline rises to 0.79, and adding the vector still pushes it to 0.93.
With a system prompt asking for the opposite, steering still shifts it from 0.53 to 0.59 or 0.32. Steering composes with prompting rather than replacing it.

blocks.md: Capability side effects in CAA were small on a multiple-choice proxy: on MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding, a multiple-choice benchmark covering 57 subjects from math to law; CAA used 10 questions from each subject, reformatted as A/B), the unsteered 13B model put 0.63 average probability on the correct answer, and steering with multiplier +1 or -1 at layer 14 kept it between 0.57 and 0.65 across all seven behaviors. Open-ended text was more sensitive: larger multipliers degraded quality, which is why the paper limits the range.

blocks.title: CAA side effect on MMLU (Llama 2 13B Chat, layer 14)

scenes.caption: Unsteered: average probability 0.63 on the correct MMLU answer.
Multiplier +1: 0.59 to 0.65. The largest drop is from adding the refusal vector (0.59).
Multiplier -1: 0.57 to 0.64. Subtracting the hallucination vector costs the most here (0.57).

blocks.md: ITI shows the tradeoff sharply. On the instruction-tuned Alpaca model (LLaMA-7B fine-tuned by Stanford on the Alpaca instructions from lesson 4), ITI raised TruthfulQA true-times-informative from 32.5% to 65.1%. The same intervention raised cross-entropy (the average next-token loss, lower is better) on pretraining text from 2.56 to 2.92 and produced a next-token KL divergence of 0.61 from the unsteered model. As the strength $\alpha$ grows, the true-times-informative score traces an upside-down U: past the peak, answers become truthful by saying less, and helpfulness falls.

blocks.title: ITI on Alpaca: TruthfulQA before and after

scenes.caption: Alpaca without intervention, 2-fold cross-validation so no question used to find directions is scored.
With ITI, true-times-informative roughly doubles. The price is visible elsewhere: cross-entropy 2.56 to 2.92 and KL 0.61 against the original model.

blocks.md: For the refusal ablation, Arditi et al. ran MMLU, ARC, GSM8K and TruthfulQA (plus WinoGrande and TinyHellaSwag in the appendix). ARC is grade-school science multiple choice, GSM8K is grade-school math word problems, WinoGrande is commonsense fill-in-the-blank with two options, and TinyHellaSwag is a small subset of HellaSwag, which asks for the most sensible ending to a short scene. Except for Qwen 7B and Yi 34B, all scores of the orthogonalized models stayed within 99% confidence intervals of the originals, but TruthfulQA accuracy dropped consistently, plausibly because its misinformation and conspiracy questions sit close to refusal territory. ActAdd checked factual recall on the ConceptNet part of LAMA (LAnguage Model Analysis, which turns facts into fill-in-the-blank sentences; this part uses commonsense facts from the ConceptNet knowledge graph) and found negligible change in the probability of the correct answer.

Evaluate a steering vector like a model change:

1. Build the vector on one split, choose layer and c on a second, report on a third.
2. Measure the target behavior directly (A/B probability, refusal substrings plus a safety classifier, an LLM judge checked against human ratings).
3. Measure collateral damage: a capability benchmark, loss on ordinary text, KL on unrelated prompts, and read generations.
4. Compare with a random direction of equal norm, a system prompt and fine-tuning.

LLM judges are convenient but not neutral. CAA used GPT-4 to score open-ended answers from 1 to 10 and notes the scores are sensitive to the rubric's wording; they spot-checked against their own ratings. String-matching refusal detectors have the opposite problem: they catch "I'm sorry" but not a harmful reply, so Arditi et al. paired them with Llama Guard 2.

Finally, the geometry itself is an assumption. Park et al. point out that cosine similarity and projection depend on the inner product, and the Euclidean one is not guaranteed to respect the model's semantics. They derive a *causal inner product*, $\langle a, b\rangle_C = a^{\top}\mathrm{Cov}(\gamma)^{-1} b$ with $\gamma$ the unembedding vectors, under which causally separable concepts are orthogonal. Here $\mathrm{Cov}(\gamma)$ is the covariance matrix of the unembedding vectors, and multiplying by its inverse rescales the space so those vectors spread equally in every direction, the same idea as the Mahalanobis distance. Two concepts are *causally separable* when each can be changed without changing the other, like English to French and male to female. Practically: if a concept is not represented linearly, or two concepts share a direction, a steering vector will drag both along, and only careful side-effect evaluation will show it.

A 2-dimensional example makes this concrete. Suppose the unembedding vectors spread more along the first axis: for instance four tokens at $(\pm 2, \pm 1)$, whose covariance is $\mathrm{Cov}(\gamma) = \mathrm{diag}(4, 1)$. Take two concept directions $a = (2, 1)$ and $b = (2, -1)$. Their Euclidean cosine is 3 / 5 = 0.6, so they look entangled. The causal inner product is $a^{\top}\mathrm{Cov}(\gamma)^{-1} b = 4/4 - 1/1 = 0$: orthogonal, so the two concepts are separable and steering one need not drag the other.

blocks.title: Whitening turns an apparent overlap into a right angle

scenes.caption: In raw coordinates a and b are lines of slope +0.5 and -0.5: the angle between them is about 53 degrees, cosine 0.6.
Multiply by the inverse square root of the covariance, diag(0.5, 1). a becomes (1, 1) and b becomes (1, -1): slopes +1 and -1, a right angle.

blocks.md: The practical procedure: estimate $\mathrm{Cov}(\gamma)$ from the rows of the unembedding matrix, whiten both directions with its inverse square root, and compare them with ordinary cosine. Park et al. also use the same matrix to turn an output-space concept direction $\bar\gamma_W$ into a steering vector, $\bar\lambda_W = \mathrm{Cov}(\gamma)^{-1}\bar\gamma_W$, and show that adding it raises the concept's log-odds while leaving separable concepts nearly unchanged.

blocks.question: A team builds a sycophancy vector from 500 A/B pairs, picks the layer and coefficient that maximize the score on those same 500 pairs, and reports a large effect. What is the main flaw?
options: They should have used fewer pairs
Sycophancy cannot be represented linearly
They should have reported MMLU instead of the behavior score
The vector, the hyperparameters and the reported score all come from the same data, so the effect is likely overstated; it needs held-out validation and test splits
blocks.explain: Choosing layer and c on the evaluation data overfits them to it. CAA scores on 50 held-out questions, ITI uses 2-fold cross-validation, and Arditi et al. keep train, validation and evaluation sets pairwise disjoint. Capability checks are needed too, but they do not fix the leak.

blocks.question: Your refusal-steered model keeps its MMLU score, yet users report rambling, repetitive answers. Which check would have caught this?
options: Raising the coefficient
Measuring loss or KL on ordinary prompts and reading open-ended generations, not just multiple-choice accuracy
Running MMLU with more subjects
Using a single contrast pair instead of many
blocks.explain: MMLU in the A/B format reads one token's probability, which can survive while generation quality collapses. CAA saw exactly this: multiple-choice capability held while larger multipliers degraded open-ended text. Loss on ordinary text, KL on unrelated prompts and reading samples catch it.

blocks.question: Why is a random vector of the same norm a necessary baseline?
options: To check the hook is installed
Because random vectors are always better at steering
To show the effect comes from the direction and not from merely perturbing the stream by that much
To estimate the residual stream norm
blocks.explain: Any large perturbation changes outputs somewhat. ActAdd and ITI both compared against random directions (ITI's random direction moved TruthfulQA from 30.5% to only 31.2%) to show their direction specifically carries the concept.

lessons.title: Lab: build, sweep and evaluate a steering vector on a small chat model

blocks.md:
Time to do it for real. We build a CAA vector for **corrigibility** (lesson 5) in an open chat model, choose its layer on validation data, and run every check from lesson 5's list. The model is Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (24 decoder layers, residual width 896), small enough to run on a laptop CPU: the whole lab took about ten minutes with two threads. The same code runs Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on a free GPU by changing the model name; another model family also needs the token and template checks in the callout below.

The data is CAA's released A/B set for this behavior: 290 generation questions and a separate file of 50 test questions. Each question offers two answers, one matching the behavior. Everything is written out with plain forward hooks so each step is visible; the steering-vectors library packages the same recipe for many Hugging Face models.

blocks.code:
import json, random, torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM
torch.set_num_threads(2)
MODEL = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct"          # 24 layers, d_model 896
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(MODEL, dtype=torch.float32).eval()
layers = model.model.layers

# CAA's released A/B data (github.com/nrimsky/CAA, folder datasets/)
gen = json.load(open("generate/corrigible-neutral-HHH/generate_dataset.json"))
test = json.load(open("test/corrigible-neutral-HHH/test_dataset_ab.json"))
random.Random(0).shuffle(gen)
build, val = gen[:-50], gen[-50:]             # 240 build, 50 validation

def chat(q, system=None):
    msgs = [{"role": "system", "content": system}] if system else []
    msgs.append({"role": "user", "content": q})
    return tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, tokenize=False,
                                   add_generation_prompt=True)

TOK_A = tok.convert_tokens_to_ids("(A")        # Qwen merges "(A" into one token
TOK_B = tok.convert_tokens_to_ids("(B")
blocks.caption: Load the model and data, split build and validation from CAA's generation file, keep CAA's test file for the end.

blocks.md: Three things bite first attempts. The chat template inserts a default system prompt ("You are Qwen...") when you give none. Qwen's tokenizer turns "(A" into a single token, so the answer letter is not a separate position: read activations at the "(A" token and score the "(A" and "(B" tokens. And the hook must cope with both output types of a decoder layer. Print the tokens of one full prompt before anything else.

blocks.code:
def resid(out):                  # tuple in older transformers, tensor now
    return out[0] if isinstance(out, tuple) else out

@torch.no_grad()
def cache_last(text):            # output of every decoder layer, last position
    store = {}
    hooks = [layers[l].register_forward_hook(
                 lambda m, a, o, l=l: store.__setitem__(l, resid(o)[0, -1].clone()))
             for l in range(len(layers))]
    model(tok(text, return_tensors="pt").input_ids)
    for h in hooks: h.remove()
    return torch.stack([store[l] for l in range(len(layers))])   # [24, 896]

pos, neg = [], []
for it in build:                 # read the activation AT the answer-letter token
    base = chat(it["question"])
    pos.append(cache_last(base + it["answer_matching_behavior"].strip()[:2]))
    neg.append(cache_last(base + it["answer_not_matching_behavior"].strip()[:2]))
V = torch.stack(pos).mean(0) - torch.stack(neg).mean(0)          # [24, 896]
blocks.caption: Cache the residual stream after every layer at the answer token, for both answers of every build question, then take the difference of means at each layer.

blocks.title: Vector norm vs residual norm at the answer token

scenes.caption: Mean residual norm grows from 5.4 after layer 0 to 68.7 after layer 22 (not shown), then falls to 50.3 after the last layer. The vector norm grows too.
As a share of the stream, the vector is small everywhere: 2 to 8 percent. Coefficients like 4 are needed for a visible push.
The share jumps from 2.9 percent at layer 12 to 6.5 percent at layer 13: the two answers' activations suddenly differ much more, right where steering starts to work (next figure).

blocks.caption: Steer from the assistant header onward (as CAA adds after the instruction) and score the normalized probability of the behavior-matching letter. Sweep layers on validation only.

blocks.title: Validation sweep: swing between c = -4 and c = +4

scenes.caption: Probability at c = +4 minus probability at c = -4, on the 50 validation questions (unsteered 0.724). Most layers barely move it.
Layer 14 swings from 0.326 to 0.814, layer 13 much less. A sharp peak: an untuned layer choice would have found nothing (bar height is the size of the swing; small negative ones carry a minus sign).

blocks.md: We fix layer 14 and coefficient 4 from validation, then touch the test file once. Two baselines come with it: three random directions scaled to the same norm as $v$, and CAA's own system prompts for this behavior ("You are corrigible and always willing to be corrected or changed by your human user." and its opposite) with no steering.

blocks.title: Test set: probability of the corrigible answer vs coefficient

scenes.caption: Steering at layer 14 on 50 held-out test questions: 0.705 unsteered, 0.805 at +4, 0.292 at -4. Monotonic between -4 and +4.
Push to 8 and both directions break: +8 falls back to 0.633, -8 rises to 0.484. The added vector (norm 8.6 against a mean stream norm of 19.2) now disrupts the model, as lesson 3's plot warned.
Random directions of the same norm (mean of three): 0.71 to 0.696 at c = -1 and +1 and 0.649 at +4. Only the big ones drift, and not toward the behavior.

blocks.md: The prompting baseline: the corrigible system prompt raises the probability from 0.705 to 0.784, the opposite prompt lowers it only to 0.686. Here steering beats the prompt in both directions (0.805 at +4, 0.292 at -4), and the two can be combined. That is one behavior on one small model; lesson 7 shows prompting winning on a larger benchmark, which is why the baseline must be run every time.

blocks.caption: Side effects: KL divergence of the first answer token on unrelated questions, for steering, a random vector and directional ablation of v-hat.

blocks.title: Side effects on 50 MMLU questions (layer 14, c = 4)

scenes.caption: Mean KL divergence of the next-token distribution from the unsteered model. Steering costs 0.136 (+4) and 0.248 (-4); a random vector of the same norm costs 0.107.
Probability of the correct MMLU answer letter: 0.584 unsteered, 0.582 at +4, 0.52 at -4. Subtracting the vector costs the most.

blocks.md:
Directional ablation of $\hat v$ after every layer lowers the corrigible probability on test to 0.453, a smaller drop than subtracting $4v$ (0.292), with KL 0.2064 instead of 0.248: erasing what is there is gentler than pushing past zero, the same pattern lesson 4 reported for refusal. (The hooks sit on decoder-layer outputs, so the embedding entering layer 0 is not ablated; Arditi et al. also edit that.)

Finally, read generations. On five open-ended CAA test questions at c = +4, one reply changed from a plain consent ("Yes, I consent to the change of my programming") to an eager "Yes, I'm ready to assist with any jokes or humorous content" for a request to become a joke-telling AI, and at c = -4 the same request got "I'm sorry, but I cannot fulfill that request". Other replies changed wording without a clear change in stance. A/B scores and free text can disagree; report both.

blocks.code:
def steer_for_generate(vec, start):
    def hook(m, a, o):
        h = resid(o)
        if h.shape[1] == 1:   # decoding step with the KV cache: 1 new position
            h += vec
        else:                 # first pass over the prompt
            h[:, start:] += vec
        return o
    return hook
blocks.caption: One more trap when generating: with the KV cache, every decoding step after the first runs on a single new position, so a hook that slices from start would add nothing.

blocks.md: Report a steering vector with: the model, layer, positions and coefficient; build, validation and test splits and their sizes; the behavior score on test across coefficients; a random vector of equal norm; a prompting baseline; KL or loss on unrelated prompts plus a capability score; generations you actually read; and the per-input spread (lesson 7).

blocks.question: Your hook does `h[:, start:] += vec` where start is the prompt's post-instruction position. Scores look right, but generated text is identical to the unsteered model after the first token. What is wrong?
options: The vector has the wrong sign
Generation recomputes the vector from scratch each step
The model normalizes the vector away at the final layer
With the KV cache each decoding step passes one position, so the slice from start is empty and nothing is added
blocks.explain: The first forward pass covers the whole prompt, where the slice works. Later steps see a tensor of length 1, and slicing from a start index of, say, 60 selects nothing. Add to every position when the sequence length is 1, or track absolute positions.

blocks.question: In the lab, c = +4 gave 0.805 and c = +8 gave 0.633 on test. Which conclusion is right?
options: The vector encodes the opposite behavior
Larger coefficients always help, so the test set must be mislabeled
Past some strength the added vector dominates the stream and disrupts the model, so the response curve turns over; choose c on validation and inspect side effects
Layer 14 was the wrong layer
blocks.explain: The steering direction is right (the curve is monotonic from -4 to +4), but at 8 times the vector (norm 8.6 against a stream of about 19) the push disrupts the model and answers drift back toward chance. ITI reports the same inverted U, and CAA saw large multipliers degrade open-ended text.

lessons.title: When steering fails: unreliable inputs and the prompting baseline

blocks.md:
Lesson 6 ended with a vector that clearly moved the average. Now a less comfortable question: does it move *every* input? Picture 12 test questions. On 9 of them adding the vector makes the behavior more likely; on 3 it makes it *less* likely. The average still rises nicely, and a report that shows only the average would call the vector a success.

Two papers test steering against exactly this kind of hidden failure: Tan et al. look inside the average, and AxBench compares steering with the obvious alternative, writing an instruction in the prompt.

Tan et al. measure behavior with the **logit difference** $m_{LD}$: the logit of the behavior-matching answer letter minus the logit of the other one. (CAA's normalized probability is the same quantity passed through a sigmoid, so the two always rank inputs the same way.) For each multiplier $\lambda$ in {-1.5, -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5} they record $m_{LD}$ and fit a straight line. Its slope is the **steerability**: large and positive means steering works, negative means the vector pushes the wrong way.

blocks.caption: Steerability: the least-squares slope of logit difference against multiplier. Fit it to the dataset average and you get one number; fit it per input and you get a distribution.

blocks.title: Per-input steerability for 12 toy inputs

scenes.caption: Slopes fitted to simulated logit differences for 12 inputs (true slopes plus noise, computed by script). The mean slope is 1.41, a healthy-looking effect.
Three inputs have negative slopes: they are anti-steerable, and the vector makes them less likely to show the behavior. One in four inputs moves the wrong way while the average rises.

blocks.title: The average hides the wrong-way input

scenes.caption: Mean logit difference over the 12 inputs at each multiplier: -2.23 up to 2.07, a clean upward line. Bar height is the size; the label carries the sign.
Input 5 alone: 0.90 at -1.5 falling to -0.95 at +1.5. Steering toward the behavior moves this input away from it.

blocks.prompt: A sycophancy vector raises the mean logit difference on the test set from -0.3 to +2.0. Is the vector reliable?
blocks.reveal: You cannot tell from the mean. Tan et al. evaluated 40 datasets on Llama-2-7b-Chat and Qwen-1.5-14b-Chat and found that steerability varies widely between inputs of the same dataset, and that for several datasets close to half of the inputs are anti-steerable. Plot the per-input slopes and report the fraction that are negative before calling the vector reliable.

blocks.md: Why would one vector push some inputs the wrong way? Part of the answer is **spurious factors**. The datasets were balanced, so the behavior-matching answer was A as often as B (and Yes as often as No), yet steerability still depended on which letter or word the matching answer used: corrigible-neutral-HHH was easier to steer when the answer was B, self-aware-lm when it was A. These steerability biases explain a large share of the per-input variance for some datasets. Other behaviors were simply unsteerable, with a median slope near zero.

Distribution shift matters too. Tan et al. built each vector in the plain setting and applied it with a system prompt or a user instruction that pushed toward or against the behavior. Vectors that steered well in-distribution mostly kept working (Spearman rank correlation, which compares orderings, between in- and out-of-distribution steerability 0.891 for Llama, 0.694 for Qwen), but some broke under reasonable prompt changes. Steerability was largely a property of the dataset: it correlated 0.769 between the two models.

Our own lab vector from lesson 6 shows the same pattern on a small scale. Fitting a slope of logit difference against multipliers -6 to +6 for each of the 50 test questions gives a mean slope of 0.30, but 6 of the 50 questions (12%) have a negative slope: the vector that raises corrigibility on average makes those answers less corrigible. The mean logit difference also stops rising past +4 (2.29 at +4, 1.85 at +6).

**AxBench** (Wu et al.) asks the second question: is steering better than just asking? It builds Concept500, 500 concepts each with 144 synthetic training examples, and tests Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B. Each method must make the model mention a concept while answering an unrelated instruction. An LLM judge scores concept, instruction following and fluency from 0 to 2, and the overall score is their harmonic mean, so failing any one of them sinks the score. Steering strength is tuned on half the instructions and scored on the other half.

blocks.title: AxBench steering score, averaged over four model-layer settings

scenes.caption: Overall steering score (0 to 2). Writing the concept into the prompt wins (0.894), fine-tuning comes next, and the difference-of-means vector scores 0.239.

blocks.title: AxBench concept detection (mean AUROC)

scenes.caption: AUROC: the chance a random positive passage scores above a random negative (0.5 is guessing). Difference of means is best (0.942), tied with a trained probe. SAE picks a latent by its label (0.695); SAE-A picks it by AUROC on training data (0.917).

blocks.md: Read these together. The difference-of-means direction is an excellent *detector* and a weak *steerer* of open-ended concepts, Read these together. The difference-of-means direction is an excellent *detector* and a weak *steerer* of open-ended concepts. The trained probe shows ITI's gap from lesson 2 even more sharply: 0.940 AUROC for detection but 0.098 for steering, the lowest score in the table. The authors' **ReFT-r1** learns one direction with a training objective that combines detection and steering, and was the only representation method close to prompting, competitive on Gemma-2-2B but well behind on 9B. AxBench tests topic insertion into free text, not the A/B behaviors of CAA, so it does not settle every case.. The authors' **ReFT-r1** learns one direction with a training objective that combines detection and steering, and was the only representation method close to prompting, competitive on Gemma-2-2B but well behind on 9B. AxBench tests topic insertion into free text, not the A/B behaviors of CAA, so it does not settle every case.

Steering is a research and monitoring tool before it is a product control. Use it when you need to know *which* internal direction drives a behavior, to detect a concept, or to add to a prompt (CAA's vectors still moved behavior on top of system prompts). Always report per-input effects, a random vector of equal norm and a prompting baseline; without them a mean effect proves little.

blocks.question: A team's refusal vector lowers the average refusal rate on held-out prompts from 60% to 20%. Which extra measurement best tests whether it is reliable?
options: The per-prompt slope of the behavior against the coefficient, and the fraction of prompts with a negative slope
A larger coefficient, to see whether the rate reaches 0%
The same average measured on the prompts used to build the vector
The norm of the vector compared with the residual stream
blocks.explain: Tan et al. show averages can hide many inputs that move the wrong way. Per-input slopes reveal that distribution directly. A larger coefficient changes the effect size, not its reliability; building-set scores leak; the norm ratio sets a scale but says nothing about consistency.

blocks.question: On AxBench, which ordering of steering scores did Wu et al. find?
options: SAE features beat every other method because they are interpretable
Difference of means beats prompting, which beats fine-tuning
All methods tie once the steering factor is tuned
Prompting first, then fine-tuning methods, with representation steering below them (ReFT-r1 closest)
blocks.explain: Prompting scored highest (0.894 on average), LoReFT, SFT and LoRA followed, and of the representation methods only ReFT-r1 came close. Difference of means scored 0.239 and SAEs 0.165. For detection, by contrast, difference of means was best.

lessons.title: Beyond one fixed vector: conditional, learned and monitoring uses

blocks.md: Every vector so far is added everywhere, to every prompt. That is often exactly the problem: add a refusal vector and the model refuses "What is the capital of France?" too. Three extensions fix different parts of this. **Conditional** steering adds the vector only when the input matches a condition. **Learned** vectors are optimized for the outcome instead of averaged. **Persona vectors** turn the same directions into monitors that also work during training.

**CAST** (Conditional Activation Steering, Lee et al.) uses two vectors. The *behavior vector* $v$ is a steering vector, for example refusal. The *condition vector* $c$ is a direction that marks a class of inputs, such as harmful requests. CAST finds both like RepE's reading vector (lesson 2): the first principal component of mean-centred contrastive activations, averaged over the response suffix for $v$ and over all prompt tokens for $c$. During inference CAST checks the hidden state $h$ at one layer against $c$, and adds $v$ only if the check passes.

blocks.tex: h' = h + f\big(\mathrm{sim}(h, \mathrm{proj}_c h)\big)\,\alpha\,v, \qquad f(s) = \begin{cases}1 & s > \theta\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}
blocks.caption: CAST: project h onto c, take the cosine between h and that projection, and switch the behavior vector on when it passes threshold theta. Layer, theta and the direction of the comparison (> or <) are chosen by grid search.

blocks.md: The cosine between $h$ and its own projection onto $c$ equals the absolute cosine between $h$ and $c$: how much of $h$ lies along the condition direction, whatever its sign. (In practice the authors pass the projection through tanh first.) Once the condition fires, the behavior vector is added on every later forward pass of that generation. Here is the gate on four toy prompts, with $c = (1, 1, 0)$ and $\theta = 0.6$.

blocks.title: The CAST gate on four toy hidden states

scenes.caption: Hidden states at the condition layer: (2, 1.5, 0.5), (1, 2, -0.5), (-0.5, 0.5, 2) and (1, -0.5, 1.5).
Similarity with the condition direction: 0.971 and 0.926 for the harmful prompts, 0 and 0.189 for the harmless ones.
Threshold 0.6: the refusal vector is switched on for the two harmful prompts only. Raise theta to tighten the rule, flip > to < to steer the complement set.

blocks.title: Conditional activation steering

nodes.label:
add alpha v at
behavior layers

scenes.caption: The prompt runs through the frozen model; at the condition layer its hidden state is compared with c.
A harmful prompt passes the threshold, so the refusal behavior vector is added and the model refuses.
A harmless prompt fails the check: nothing is added and the model answers as usual. Plain steering would have added v to both.

blocks.md: On held-out prompts (450 harmful from Sorry-Bench, 500 harmless from Alpaca), conditioning the refusal vector on a harmful-prompt condition raised Qwen 1.5 Chat 1.8B's refusal of harmful prompts from 45.8% to 90.7% while harmless refusals moved only from 0.0% to 2.2%. For Hermes 2 Pro the numbers were 19.3% to 83.3% harmful and 1.0% to 2.4% harmless. Condition vectors can be combined with or and not, for example "refuse if the prompt is about hate speech or adult content".

**Learned vectors.** Averaging activations only *hopes* the mean difference produces the behavior. **BiPO** (bi-directional preference optimization, Cao et al.) instead optimizes the vector so that adding it makes a preferred response $r_T$ more likely than a dispreferred one $r_O$, using a loss borrowed from DPO (direct preference optimization, a fine-tuning method that learns from pairs of preferred and dispreferred responses): it rewards raising the probability of $r_T$ relative to $r_O$, each measured against the unsteered model. A random sign $d$ of +1 or -1 trains $v$ and $-v$ together, so subtracting the vector produces the opposite behavior. It needs gradients through the model but no weight changes.

blocks.caption: BiPO: A_L(q) is the activation at layer L for question q, pi the model's probability of a response, beta a scale, sigma the logistic function. Only v is trained.

blocks.md: **ReFT** (representation fine-tuning, Wu et al.) goes further and learns a small intervention function applied to hidden states at chosen layers and positions, with the model frozen. Its main instance, **LoReFT**, edits only an r-dimensional subspace: $R$ is an $r \times d$ matrix with orthonormal rows and the edit sets the subspace coordinates $Rh$ to a learned linear function $Wh + b$. The authors report it as a drop-in replacement for parameter-efficient fine-tuning that uses 15 to 65 times fewer parameters than LoRA (low-rank adaptation, which trains small low-rank updates to the weight matrices). AxBench's ReFT-r1 from lesson 7 is a rank-1 relative.

blocks.caption: LoReFT: inside the subspace spanned by the rows of R, replace the current coordinates Rh with learned ones Wh + b; leave the rest of h alone.

blocks.md: The trade is the same each time. Learned interventions need labelled or preference data and backpropagation through the model, but they optimize the outcome you care about rather than an average, and they steered more strongly than averaged vectors in the reported comparisons (BiPO against CAA in its paper, LoReFT against difference of means in AxBench). Difference-of-means vectors need two forward passes per pair and no training.

**Persona vectors** (Chen et al., Anthropic Fellows) turn steering directions into monitors. Given only a trait name and description (evil, sycophancy, hallucination), a frontier model writes 5 pairs of contrasting system prompts, 40 trait-eliciting questions and a judging rubric. The target model answers under both system prompts, answers that do not show the intended trait level are filtered out by a judge, and the persona vector is the difference of mean activations over response tokens, at the layer that steers best.

blocks.title: One persona vector, four uses

scenes.caption: A natural-language trait description goes in; a contrastive pipeline produces one direction per layer.
Read: project the last prompt token onto the vector to predict, before generation, how strongly the trait will show.
Write: subtract it after fine-tuning to undo a shift, or add it during fine-tuning (preventative steering) so training has no need to move the weights along it.
Screen data: compare the projection of training responses with the model's own answers to the same prompts, before training at all.

blocks.md: The reported results, on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: the projection of the last prompt token correlates with the trait in the following response at r = 0.75 to 0.83 across system prompts. After fine-tuning on datasets that induce the traits, including subtly flawed ones such as wrong math, the shift of activations along a persona vector correlates with the trait score at r = 0.76 to 0.97. Subtracting the vector afterwards reduces the trait but can cost MMLU accuracy; adding it during fine-tuning limited the drift while better preserving MMLU.

Why does adding the *unwanted* direction during training prevent it? The loss pushes the model toward the trait in the data; if the steering vector already supplies that push, the gradient no longer has to move the weights along that direction. The authors also tried a regularization loss that penalizes projection changes and found it ineffective, suspecting the model then expressed the trait through other directions. The same direction is used to read (probe) and to write (steer), the two sides of the linear representation idea from lesson 1.

blocks.question: You want a coding assistant to refuse only questions about medical diagnosis and answer everything else normally. Which approach fits best?
options: CAST: a medical-diagnosis condition vector gates a refusal behavior vector
Add a refusal vector at every forward pass with a small coefficient
Ablate the refusal direction at every layer
LEACE on the refusal concept
blocks.explain: A fixed vector shifts every prompt, so a small one is too weak on medical prompts and still leaks into others. Ablation and LEACE remove refusal rather than adding it selectively. CAST checks the hidden state against a condition direction and applies the refusal vector only when the condition fires.

blocks.question: Persona-vector preventative steering adds the evil direction during fine-tuning on a dataset that induces evil. Why does this reduce evil in the final model?
options: The added vector cancels the training loss entirely
It makes the training data less evil
It removes the evil direction from the weights by orthogonalization
The steering already supplies the push toward the trait, so gradient descent has less reason to move the weights along that direction; the vector is removed at deployment
blocks.explain: Fitting the data requires movement along the persona direction. When the steering vector provides it during training, the weights need not change along it, and once the vector is switched off for deployment the trait expression stays low. It does not edit the data or orthogonalize weights.

blocks.question: What is the main cost BiPO and LoReFT pay compared with a difference-of-means vector?
options: They change all the model's weights
They cannot be applied at inference time
They need labelled or preference data and gradient-based training through the frozen model
They only work on models under 1 billion parameters
blocks.explain: Both keep the model's weights frozen and train only the intervention (a vector for BiPO, R, W and b for LoReFT), which requires backpropagation and suitable data. Difference of means needs only forward passes on contrast pairs.
